## The idea

The lowest sounding note strongly influences how a chord is heard. Put each
root on a downbeat and the harmony becomes clear. It also becomes predictable.
A bass line gains direction when it connects those structural roots with
passing tones, chord tones, and *approach notes*, pitches a semitone above or
below the next target.

Start with the dull version. It is the test fixture. If the root bass does not
state the progression clearly, decoration will hide the problem. Then keep the
same downbeat targets and change the path between them.

Rhythmic independence is as important as pitch choice. A bass that copies every
melody duration behaves like the bottom of a chord voicing. Give it sustained
downbeats, a walking quarter-note pulse, or a syncopated anticipation that the
melody does not share.

## Run this

The progression is C, A minor, F, G. The first pass plays roots on downbeats.
The second uses four quarter notes per bar and approaches the next root from
one semitone below.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :fm

roots = [note(:c2), note(:a1), note(:f1), note(:g1)]

define :play_root_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each do |root|
    play root, release: 3.6, amp: 0.7
    sleep 4
  end
end

define :play_walking_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each_with_index do |root, index|
    next_root = root_notes[(index + 1) % root_notes.length]
    fifth = root + 7
    passing = root + (next_root > root ? 4 : -3)
    approach = next_root - 1

    [root, fifth, passing, approach].each do |pitch|
      play pitch, release: 0.75, amp: 0.7
      sleep 1
    end
  end
end

play_root_bass roots
sleep 2
play_walking_bass roots
```

The first pass marks four harmonic pillars. The second keeps those pillars on
the downbeats while its final note in each bar leans into the next root.

## Change one thing

1. Replace approach = next_root - 1 with approach = next_root + 1. The approach
   now falls into the target from above. Compare which direction sounds more
   natural before each root.
2. Change fifth to root + 12. The octave is stable but less harmonically
   informative than the fifth. Listen for the line becoming wider and more
   repetitive.
3. In play_walking_bass, change the four sleeps to [1.5, 0.5, 1, 1] by zipping
   pitches with that duration array. The bar total stays four, while the bass
   acquires a rhythm distinct from a quarter-note melody.

## Why it works

Downbeat roots define the chord sequence because bass register gives them
perceptual weight. The notes between roots can create local tension as long as
the structural targets arrive on time. A chromatic approach note is outside the
current chord for one beat, but its half-step resolution explains its role.

Passing tones work best when they describe a clear route. Between roots a third
apart, one scale step fills the gap. Between more distant targets, prefer chord
tones on stronger beats and reserve unstable notes for weak beats. This is a
constraint system, not a list of allowed pitches.

The code keeps roots as data and computes the connective material in one
function. That makes the root bass a regression test for the walking version.
If a computed line lands on the wrong downbeat, inspect the indexing or the
duration sum before changing individual pitches.

Register needs a lower bound. Notes that are clear on piano can turn to rumble
on an FM or sub-bass synth. Raise the whole line an octave before cutting its
volume. The issue may be spectral density rather than amplitude.

## Take it further

Choose an eight-bar progression from an earlier harmony lesson. Render it first
with one root per bar, then with a walking line that preserves every downbeat
root. Require at least four chromatic approaches and four diatonic passing
tones, label each in comments, and give the walking line a rhythm the melody
does not use. The answer should include a bar-total check and both versions
played in sequence for direct comparison.
